title: ACCA 2026 SOS three-candidate forum — Mountain View
transcriptText:
I was saying the chatter does echo in this room. This is a very important forum, I think. This is the first time I'm told that these three have debated on a stage together. Everyone's going to want to hear what they're saying, so if you do have any side conversations, please take those outside. I expect this will take up the full two hours allotted, so there won't be any breaks. If you need to get up and go, you don't have to ask permission, just go. All right. Good afternoon, and welcome to today's Candidate Forum. My name is Lindsey French, and I will serve as moderator for this event. The purpose of today's forum is to provide Arkansas county clerks and election professionals with an opportunity to hear directly from the candidates for Secretary of State, and learn about their qualifications, priorities, and vision for serving the citizens of Arkansas. As county clerks, your offices play a critical role in conducting elections, maintaining voter registration records, assisting candidates, and ensuring public confidence in our electoral process. The Secretary of State's office serves an important partner to county officials in carrying out these responsibilities, making this election particularly relevant to the work you all do every day. I want to thank the candidates for their time and willingness to participate and travel to this forum. We're pleased to welcome the candidates for Arkansas Secretary of State, Kelly Graff, Kim Hammer, and Dr. Michael Pacco. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Before we begin, I'd like to review the format for today's forum. Opening statement order was determined by random draw. The order of responses to questions will rotate throughout the forum to ensure fairness. Closing statements will be given in the reverse order of the opening statements. Candidates will be given 90 seconds to answer each question, unless otherwise noted. Candidates should address the audience and moderator rather than one another. Personal attacks and interruptions will not be tolerated. Time limits will be strictly enforced to ensure equal opportunity for all candidates. To begin, we'll hear opening statements from each candidate. We've asked them to use this time to introduce themselves and share their vision for the Secretary of State's office, particularly as it relates to supporting county clerks, administering elections, and serving the people of Arkansas. First to give their opening statement is Kim Hammer. Thank you. Appreciate the opportunity to be here with you. I don't think I'm a stranger to a lot of you because I've worked with you throughout my legislative career, eight years in the House, eight years in the Senate. And people ask the question, well, why do you wanna run as Secretary of State? And the answer is pretty clear to me. Number one, and I genuinely mean this, I'm just running to find out if it's God's will that I'm supposed to move on and continue to serve the public. You don't know these things unless you put yourself out there. And so I'm just running primarily to find out, is this God's will that I should continue to serve in an elected position to be able to serve the public as I've done in the last 16 years. The other reason is because I've got 16 years of experience that I really don't wanna put up on the shelf. Some of that 16 years has had great success, some of it's had great failures, and all of it can be beneficial to continue to serve in the future. And so I'd like to take my 16 years and continue to serve Secretary of State level. As you know, I've worked with many of you throughout the legislative career. I think one of the key things that you need to have in a relationship with the Secretary of State is a working relationship where we work with you, not against you. We work together and not against each other. And that means that we come together, have the kind of meetings and discussions that before legislation is introduced, that we can at least get on the same page. And if we can't, we can at least be civil about it so that whatever our disagreements may be can be done in a healthy debate and a healthy process. So I look forward to working with you if I'm elected as your next Secretary of State. One of the things I want to make sure, too, is that you get all the support you need on the Secretary of State's office, whether that's revamping the website in order to make it more user-friendly, maybe having some interaction with our legal team when we have questions, not that we can go to court for you, but we certainly can be an ally for you because what affects you affects us. And so I think that we have to have that interaction between the clerks and between the Secretary of State's office because at the end of the day, if the voters win, we all win. And let each party and let each individual get out there and advocate for what they believe is strong. Our job is just to make sure that the elections are fair and that we keep our number one status in the nation as the most secure state in the nation to conduct elections. So I appreciate, look forward to answering the questions and a few closing comments at the end. Thank you. Thank you. Next up for opening statements, Dr. Michael Paco. Oh, thank you, thank you, it's good to be here. I appreciate the invitation that the three of us got to join you at this beautiful venue here. I'm looking forward to afterwards going out and taking in some of the sights and attractions. But in the meanwhile, my name is Michael Paco and I'm the Libertarian candidate for Secretary of State. Some of you may know me as the Arkansas economist quoted in the newspaper, appearing on TV and radio, explaining what the latest economic statistics mean for Arkansas and the Arkansas economy. But I also have a side gig for the past decade or so. I've been the chairman of the Libertarian Party of Arkansas. And from that perspective, I bring kind of an outsider's point of view to politics in Arkansas. From my point of view, it looks to me like there could be a lot more competition in our politics, not just between Republicans and Democrats, but within the Democratic Party, within the Republican Party and with third parties and independents as well. In this very hyper-partisan environment where the two parties of the duopoly accuse each other of disenfranchising voters and defrauding the system, I think that it's really important that Arkansas have a Secretary of State who can stand above the partisan bickering and stand for the people of Arkansas and support the county clerks, for that matter, in the execution and implementation of our elections. So that's kind of the angle that I bring onto it. And if you're going to kind of summarize my campaign in a bumper-sticker-type slogan, it's simply that elections are too important to leave to the Democrats and Republicans. Now, I do have more that I want to talk to about some specific reforms to our electoral process that I think would improve the competitive environment, would improve competition. And I think this audience would be a great sounding board for some of these ideas, but I don't want to take up all your time here in my opening statements. I hope we'll have a chance to talk about some of those suggestions later on. But for now, I guess that's who I am. Glad to be here, and I look forward to taking all the questions that were coming up next. And last but not least, Kelly Crowley. Thank you all for having us today. I am really honored to be in this room with you, and I'm honored to be on this stage with Dr. Paco and Senator Hammer. We just had a quick conversation that I just want to tell y'all. I'm excited about running against these two because we made a commitment to each other that we're going to do this the right way. And so I'm thankful for that. So I'm running for Secretary of State. If I have to summarize the reason I'm running for Secretary of State in one word, it's people. Because I do love this state, and I believe in the people of Arkansas. And I believe that the county clerks are a big part of why people trust our government. So your role is so critical. And my mission in this job is going to be as a service role. I'm listening. I picked up so many questions and ideas this morning just based on some of the challenges that y'all have out there. And so my number one goal is to make sure, first of all, that our elections maintain their security and their integrity just like they are today, but also to really listen and understand what we could do differently or better to support you, get barriers out of your way, make things more efficient. Because I just think there's some opportunity. I come from a background more than 30 years in the business sector. I'm not a lifetime politician. I led a team of 800 people. I ran a big building in Little Rock with the Verizon headquarters. And I just believe that this role is an administrator. It's a constitutional officer. And I have background and experience that I believe will help me make sure that you've got the support that you need in the Secretary of State's office. So my commitment to you is to listen and to really understand where your barriers are and to make sure that people feel confident in the system so that they come and plug in. I'm on a personal mission to get more people to the table when it comes to politics and to take some of the heat out of the Democrat, Republican, Libertarian, whatever you are, because at the end of the day, we're all Arkansans and we have to come back to each other and we have to be able to talk to each other and work together to move this state forward. And so I have a vision for that and I have so many great ideas I can't wait to share with you today. Thank you for having me. Thank you all. We'll begin with the questions. We will change up the order of response for each question and you'll have 90 seconds to respond. First for this question is Kim Hammer. County clerks, election staff and poll workers face increasing pressure, criticism and negativity during elections. This leads to burnout and resignation of seasoned election officials. As Secretary of State, what steps would you take to support and retain election workers across Arkansas? Thank you for the question. That's a realistic question because it's a real issue that's out there. I'll tell you a quick story. I heard from one county and you may be in the room so I hope I restated accurately, but one of their poll workers who was 93 said, I've just got to give it up or it was election coordinator said, I've just got to give it up and was replaced with a 94 year old. So that kind of indicates to you the problems that we're having. So my intent is number one, I really think the Secretary of State needs to be out in the state. It needs to be out in the office and traveling in the counties, working directly with the clerks and the other county officials as well, which are primarily because you oversee the elections. But also I think the Secretary of State needs to be in the schools. And just to be honest with you, we got an upper layer, they're very engaged. We got a middle layer of population.

that's kind of sort of, if it's convenient, engaged. And what we really need to do is being out there, to be out there and work, starting with the elementary and going up through the high school and the college, and start to create a generation that's going to come up and understand the value of being involved in the process and being out there to help. We have now a law that says you've got to have 75 hours of community service in the high school before you can graduate. We need to make a direct connection between them and working at the polls and instilling in them the understanding of the value of getting out and vote. The one thing I think... Time. Sorry, I am going to call you out so we can stay on schedule. Perfect. Next, Dr. Paco, and if anyone needs me to repeat the question, feel free to ask. Well, you know, I think I hinted at the outset that the view that the partisan bickering has really caused a conflict that really has weaponized some of our key institutions, including elections, calling into question the integrity of the elections themselves and the officials that run the elections, including all of you and the Secretary of State as well. And so I think it's important that we try to re-instill the confidence that the people of Arkansas should have in our process, that we have fair, free elections. They're well maintained, well monitored, and to some extent, if there's bad information out there about how crooked elections are, the best way to combat that is with more good information. So I would like to see an initiative statewide among all the county clerks, election coordinators, the election commission members, and the Secretary of State's office to maybe make more out of the process of we're testing the voting machines and reassuring the voters that everything's only up and up. They get a bigger vent rather than what I suspect it often is, is just a couple of Republicans or Democrats showing up to the testing process. So I think putting out a strong message to the public about the integrity of the elections from a common perspective would be a good approach. Thank you. Kelly Graham. I think there's three key things here. Number one is around civic education, which Senator Hanna alluded to. My husband and I do a civic education program for high school students. And one of the things that I've really learned through that process is that young people want to plug in, but they might not want to come to a Democratic committee meeting or a Republican committee meeting. They want to use their own God-given talents to plug into the system. And so I'm running my campaign with that philosophy. I've got a mural artist that I'm working with. I have a guy who wrote a song a couple of weeks ago. And I think we've got to find ways to help our youth plug in where they are. So that's the first thing. And we want to teach them how to plug into the system so that they can use their power and their voice. Our population, we now have more voting-age people under 50 than we do over 50. And y'all know who votes, right? Y'all know who votes. We have more people over 50. And so I'm trying to show them their power. The second thing that I think is really important is giving people something to come out for and not just against. There's so much polarization, and my whole campaign theme is people over politics. I want to help communities understand how they use our civic power to change things if they want to change things. And so that's really a critical piece of it as well. Second question. Arkansas currently utilizes paper ballots that are scanned and tabulated by machines. What are your views on continuing Arkansas' current paper ballot system versus a return to hand-marked, hand-counted paper ballots, and why? You need to know who's first. Dr. Pico, that's you. The paper ballots issue is one that, to some extent, has really puzzled me. As you pointed out in the question, we do have paper ballots in Arkansas. It's a credible, traceable, written record of the votes. Whether they're the fill-in-the-circles kind that we had in Pulaski County or the ballot marking devices that are used in other counties, there is a piece of paper that comes out of that process that, at least in the case of the ballot marking devices, the names are printed on the ballot. The voters can look at it and see that those are the people I voted for before they put it into the reader. And maybe we need to remind people that that's there, because there seems to be an awful lot of concern and complaints about that. As far as hand-counting goes, I think that's just unrealistic from the amount of labor and cost that that would be. And for that matter, I think the results of the recount in the recent election for the Secretary of State Republican candidates showed that the hand-count can be done, but you come up with the same results as the tabulating devices. So that's more efficient. And to tell you the truth, if you hand-count it, you're opening up to human error and human shenanigans, for that matter. So I think there's just as many problems with that, if not more, than there are with the way we do things now. So this has been very controversial, right? And I want to stand up here in front of all of you today and let you know that I believe our elections are so secure, just like I know you guys believe our elections are so secure. I do think there's some questions about it, and so I think transparency is an opportunity as far as, and I know that's a buzzword right now, but I think that when we show people how secure our elections are, it helps them see that, oh, I'm not as worried about that, I may not have to think about it. But the good news is that in Arkansas, it's the law that they could have hand-marked, hand-counted ballots, but they can also have the machines. And at the end of the day, as the service role, my job will be to make sure that it's secure, regardless of the system that they use. So I think our systems are secure, I think they're great, but the counties do have the opportunity to choose something different, and I've spent time with Searcy County, who has the paper ballots, and at the end of the day, we've just got to make sure that those systems are secure and that the counties have the support that they need. Personally, I think that electronic, we've got to be efficient, and it's going to be really hard to do a full-on hand-marked, hand-counted. But at the end of the day, my job as Secretary of State is to make sure that the counties have the training that they need, the processes that they need, and they're supported, as long as they're within the law. Senator Hammer? Thank you. I might have a little knowledge in this area. My position on it is, first and foremost, I'll no longer be a legislator. What we will be responsible for, whichever one of the three of us get elected, is to make sure that whatever we are given by law, the legislature signed into law by the governor, passed down by a federal initiative or a federal act, we will have to be responsible for facilitating. Where we get personally involved is, as was mentioned, we've got to give you as much support as we can, regardless of whatever you choose to do as a county. However, I would point you to California and other states that are looking at going in that direction, like Georgia, and we just talked about the manpower issue. How in the world are we going to have enough manpower to do an accurate paper count, and why would you leave a system that has gotten us to be the number one state in the nation for election integrity and security? And I would raise this issue, and this is what I've raised on the campaign trail. Point to me a candidate who legitimately could raise the argument that they lost the election because it was stolen. And you can't. You can't find it. So as a result of it, why would you want to leave a proven system that is working and leave all that in order to go back to an era that we worked so hard to get away from? We'll have the responsibility to facilitate whatever is given to us and so my position on it, personally speaking, is if it isn't broke, don't fix it, but trust and verify. And as long as we do that, we'll maintain our status as the number one state in the nation for election integrity and security. And we don't want to make your job harder as clerks understanding that we will not pass the law. We'll have to enforce the law. We don't want to make your job harder. Alright, question number three. Kelly Barrett, you'll be first this time. Arkansas is widely recognized as a national leader in election security and integrity. Why do you think Arkansas election security is so strong? And what do you think could be improved on in Arkansas elections? So I, everywhere I go, if it's during the day when y'all are at work, I try to go by the county clerk's office. And I have met with so many of y'all and I am confident in our system because I know it's being executed well locally. Elections are handled locally. The Secretary of State is a support function for you all as you're executing on that. And so I'm confident because I am meeting you and I know that your counties are, you're accountable to your counties. So that's the first thing. I do think that we need to show people how secure it is. I went to a session not long ago where we were, we heard from people about why they don't or do trust our elections. And the number one thing I heard is they trust it when they can go into the polling location and they know people. And I think that's a big deal. And you guys being there, your staff being there, the election commissioners being there makes a huge difference. But I do think that we could do some videos. I have a plan, I come from a marketing background. And so I want to show people how secure it is. I want to give them videos and I want to show how awesome that y'all are at doing this amazing work. Because at the end of the day, when people can see it for themselves, they go, oh, I get it. And if they don't think so and they have all those details and they want to change the system, then in Arkansas they have the ability to do that. And so I also want to show them that. I think it is secure. Thank you. Senator Hammer. Thank you. If you look at the legislation that's been passed, you'll see my name is primary sponsor or co-sponsor. And that's part of the reason why we are where we are as a nation. We actually took the scorecard that Heritage had whenever it was that we were not number one and we tried to align with what is it that we have to do, looking at what happens in other states. And what we did was put a lot of proactive legislation in place. We put in a lot of boxes, those kind of things, that will help prevent and keep our election from being secure. But here's the thing. Y'all are the front line. And we've got to listen to what you say in order to get it passed into law so that we can give you the tools that you need in order to make sure that we get it passed into law.

that frontline people know that what they are doing has been a participation process and then that way you can help in your local communities as was said because it's the local people that have voted you because they have confidence in you and therefore we need to support you Secretary of State. I do not think that we do enough to promote and to tell that we are the number one state in the nation and that's what they want to do Secretary of State. We have to play catch-up and not be an office that is quiet. We have to be an office that is loud because if we are loud then that puts those that have the conspiracy mentality into question and they have to play defense. We need to play offense not defense and be very aggressive about getting that message out there and that will encourage people to want to get out and vote. Thank you. Dr. Packard. Well I think the record speaks for itself that you all do a great job in administering the election so that's why we have received that ranking. I guess I would I'm not sure that a ranking from the Heritage Foundation is a definitive guide to security but I think we need to continue to speak up and be public about the process that we go through the testing that goes into the whole process as I said earlier that a kind of coordinated public relations campaign among all levels of election administration to demonstrate would be a good idea. Now you know fundamentally though I think a lot of the concerns that come up about the integrity of our election system are always about the other guy that other state where they're messing things up you know it's never our politicians are never saying well our system is rigged otherwise they'd be saying that maybe their election wasn't legitimate I suppose but you know I think we just need to hammer home the point that at least here in Arkansas we've got the situation under control and do everything we can as a team from the top down throughout the all the prisons all the election voters workers and everything to make that confidence clear to the voters. That is a great segue into our next question for Senator Hamer you'll be first this time. The Save America Act has passed the house in Washington and is currently before the U.S. Senate. While Arkansas already implements the majority of its provisions there are concerns as it relates to what type of identification must be shown to register to vote to prove citizenship. For example potential voters may have trouble obtaining a birth certificate, have issues with legal name changes, and Arkansas real IDs currently do not verify U.S. citizenship so Arkansas real ID could not be used to register to vote in Arkansas as it is currently. What is your response to the Save America Act and how would you address these concerns? Well first of all they gotta get along up there in order to get anything out and I don't know a whole lot of hope for that and the fact of the matter is that whatever they pass down will be duty bound to implement it you know and so the ball is in their court unfortunately the ball's going to end up in our court with whatever comes down the way the rules to enforce. I think that every voter needs to be a legal U.S. citizen and we also need to improvise technology that brings together all the resources in order to make sure that when somebody shows up and you look at their name in the poll book that you know that they are a legal voter. Unfortunately I don't want to speculate because until the Save Act comes down we just have to continue as we are doing and whenever the Save Act comes down we're going to have to figure out how to make it work and I think that'll be the critical relationship between the Secretary of State and the clerk's offices how is that going to shape out. On the Save Act the one thing I will say every vote counts but every vote ought to be legal and we all want that in the room because if somebody votes illegally it offsets your vote as a legal voter so as long as we all work together to make sure that those that are showing up to vote are legal and I think there are some things that have to be done internally among agencies like with the Department of Motor Vehicle and the other things where there has to be some greater cooperation and there are systems that we can bring in place to make sure that that happens that will be our focus that would be my effort is what can we do to make sure our systems are communicating with each other and the clerks are getting good pure information. Dr. Petko. Well I think I agree with Senator that the Save Act is probably unlikely to make it through Congress and get to us but if it does of course that we will be duty bound to carry out it's what it calls for but I do think that it's a really bad idea it's probably unconstitutional elections are traditionally and legally in the realm of the state and even more so they're they depend on the local the precincts the counties to carry them out there's just no room in this process for the federal government to be stepping in and telling us how we should be running our elections and you know for that matter that some of the concerns have been raised about enhanced ID requests you know enhanced IDs we have now would not be good enough under the Save Act that's just carrying things too far it's unnecessary we have ID laws here in Arkansas they allow us to verify the identity of the voters and we need to be at least somewhat flexible about what the form of those IDs are and not put additional burdens on say a married woman to have to try to find their birth certificate and the marriage certificate in order to register not the kind of hurdles we need in our election process. Kelly Grant. The Winthrop Rockefeller Institute did a civic index survey a couple of years ago and Arkansas was at the bottom of voter engagement and that to me is a failure we want more people at the table we want the right people at the table and as Senator Hammer and Dr. Paco both said we already have such secure processes here we require voter ID we require you to be a citizen that's already in place and I think there's just a lot in the media right now where they're trying to plant seeds about our elections being not secure and I just don't buy it and so I don't think that it's necessary and again I think it's going to get hung up and we're not going to have to worry about that anyway but at the end of the day we need more people at the table something a lot of people haven't really even thought about or talked about much though is the burden that this might put on the county clerks because all of a sudden you've got right now I'm out registering people to vote well now they're going to have to come in and bring documentation we're going to have to have all those systems in place and I'm worried about the administrative burden that that may put on the county clerk's office so I really want to understand that if something like this legislation goes into effect because at the end of the day you guys are managing those roles and you're the one responsible for making sure that everything is right and I just want to you know make sure that if that happens that we have the processes in place to support you Dr. Michael Paco will be the first to respond to this question the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 requires that motor vehicle registration agencies public assistance agencies and disability service agencies provide voter registration assistance to citizens the most common example is someone being asked if they want to register to vote when getting their driver's license or renewing their vehicle license at the Department of Motor Vehicles county clerks have historically had issues with these registration applications incomplete applications received applications not making it to the clerk people being registered who are not citizens or who did not really want to register etc how would you address and improve voter registration issues between state agencies and county clerks well that's a that's a tricky question because of course we want to encourage all citizens who are eligible to register to vote and to make it as easy as possible for instance at the driver's license office or wherever else they're interacting with their state or local government but I think there also needs to be adequate training and send out a memo or something that there are certain requirements that must be met if people are going to register to vote and I think you know when Cole Jester recently did this examination to see how many non-citizens were registered to vote in Arkansas I would venture to guess that nearly all of them were there accidentally because no one really told them they couldn't register to vote it wasn't some sort of conspiracy to throw the elections or anything like that so it does create problems that create suspicions and concerns so perhaps the county clerks and the secretary of state's office needs to be more proactive about making sure that the keys are crossed and the eyes are dotted when it comes to voter registration forms Helen Grant I've heard this come up a few times as I've talked to several different county clerks and the staff at the county clerk's office and it sounds like I'm a process person so in much of my time at Verizon you know Verizon big telecom company bought up a whole bunch of companies and and part of my role was to identify best practices in process and really dig into the process and make sure that those are smooth and that we're doing things as easy as possible but also as securely as possible and then training people and what I've heard is that when people come in and they register at the DMV maybe that data doesn't come over as clean as it needs to and y'all are having to do a lot of cleanup and follow-up and then you know sometimes people are getting registered because they have to they feel like they have to to get their medical benefits and so it's just kind of a half attempt at it and I think we need to dig into that process and understand how that data is coming through make sure that there's training at those other agencies so that that what you get is clean because none of us none of the agencies have extra time to be double doing work and at the end of the day we want more people registered to vote and we need to make sure that's done securely and so to me there's a system issue that I want to understand and dig under those covers and make sure that we can make that easy make sure everybody's trained and make sure you get the information that you need so you don't have to double do work. Kim Hammer. I'll use an analogy. I think we need to take you all out of the back seat, put you by the passenger window, I'll be the driver, we'll put DMV in the middle, tomorrow I'm going to have a talk. And a lot of times what I think we have to do and look I'm not I'm not a lawyer don't pretend to be don't really want to be but having a good legal staff on both sides and getting everybody in the room and saying look we got to address this because we kicked the can down the road too far as was mentioned you guys shouldn't have to be doing the work of others and shouldn't be doing cleanup work either for that matter.

But I think really what's gonna require is getting everybody in the room that has the power and the influence in order to make things happen and make the adjustments and make the changes and make the corrections. And if we have to change the law in order to give power to whoever needs to have the power, we need to get the legislature involved, get the governor on board, and work as a team. But I don't think y'all need to be in the back seat, I think you need to be in the front seat. Cuz at the end of the day, you gotta deal with people that come in and say, well, I'm registered to vote. Well, no, you aren't. Or you gotta deal with the people. And once they leave the DMV, their job is done, so we need to make sure that their job is done right. Or we need to put something in place to where it just takes it out of their hands and puts it in your hands. But we all need to be talking together in a room instead of outside a room. Thank you, Mr. President. This is question six out of ten. Kelly Graff will be the first responder on this one. Misinformation is rampant, fact-checking is far underutilized, and public confidence and trust in elections as a whole is at an all-time low. Whether it be trusting the election system, the candidates, or even whether one's vote matters at all. How would you work to improve public confidence and trust in elections? So I mentioned earlier that I have, part of my background is in marketing, and part of my background is in training, learning, and development. And I think that we need a full-blown campaign around this to help people understand and to tell them truth. And the truth has to be louder than all of the rhetoric. Right now, I think there's a general distrust in the government. There's a general distrust in whether or not it's worth it to go vote. Because is it gonna count or not? At the end of the day, we need a representative government. In order to do that, we have to get more people to the table. And so I have a plan around doing some significant marketing on how you plug into the system, how your vote matters, why the elections are secure, but then also just education around how people can plug in. There's a lot of young people that are like, I'm never gonna run for office. That's too ugly out there. Y'all heard that from young people? They're like, I'm not even gonna register to vote because I'm afraid I might have to go to jury duty. Y'all heard that? And so I think we've got to go out there and show them their power and give them some wins. Encourage young people to get out and run for office and give them the tools. It will also be to make sure that when the business sector is brought into the equation, that it is number one in customer service, because we want to take care of our citizens and we want to take care of our businesses. We want to make sure that they get good, quick, accurate information in a timely manner and that they are responded to in a manner that you and I want to be responded to as well. One thing that hasn't been discussed that needs to be put on the table to be considered also exists. Probably, with all likelihood, if history upholds itself, whoever your next Secretary of State is, is also going to be the one that would be re-elected in the second term, and we're going to be dealing with redistricting. And that is critical, and that doesn't need to be discarded or dismissed either. And so we're all in this together, and it is a bigger platform than just me or just you and your respective position. It's all of us working together. If experience matters to you, I've got 16 years of experience. Am I a career politician? If I'm a career politician, I'm not doing a lot of other things. I'm a citizen who wants to continue to serve and make myself available to you, as I hope that I've proven over the last 16 years. Have we always agreed? No, but iron sharpeneth iron, and at the end of the day, you're equipped to go out and do the job that you're called, or in our case, that you're elected to do. So I hope that you would consider supporting me in your individual capacity, and I thank you for today's opportunity. And I thank you for the other two that are in the race. I hope we've conducted ourselves in a manner that makes you proud of Arkansas politics.
